cues.text: Section eight: Operational efficiency through IT.
Operational efficiency means delivering the desired outputs with less waste, time, cost or error, while maintaining quality.
It is different from effectiveness.
Effectiveness means achieving the right outcome.
Consider this carefully: a team can efficiently process the wrong applications.
Efficiency without effectiveness is not success.
Now let us separate three ideas that are often confused.
Automation executes repetitive tasks.
Integration connects systems.
Optimisation improves how resources are used.
Keep in mind that digitising a paper form does not necessarily remove redundant approvals.
So process redesign may be required before automation.
Let us look at a table that links six dimensions of efficiency to an example and a measure.
I will go row by row.
First, the dimension of speed.
The example is automated order processing, and the measure is cycle time.
Second, cost.
The example is reduced manual reconciliation, and the measure is cost per transaction.
Third, quality.
The example is validation at data entry, and the measure is error rate.
Fourth, resource use.
The example is route optimisation, and the measure is fuel per delivery.
Fifth, visibility.
The example is real-time dashboards, and the measure is reporting delay.
Sixth, scalability.
The example is elastic infrastructure, and the measure is throughput at peak demand.
Notice that each dimension pairs an improvement with something you can actually measure.
Now consider a Lagos logistics firm.
Manual dispatch relies on phone calls and paper manifests.
GPS tracking, route optimisation, automatic customer notifications and a central dashboard can reduce uncertainty, idle time and failed deliveries.
But the firm must also redesign its dispatch procedures, train drivers, and provide fallback mechanisms for when connectivity fails.
Next, data-driven operations.
These use measured evidence instead of guesswork.
The cycle is this: collect reliable events, integrate them, analyse patterns, decide, act, and monitor the result.
A good example is predictive inventory forecasting, which uses historical demand and other signals to estimate future stock requirements.
The balance matters here.
Too much stock ties up capital, while too little loses sales.
And forecasts must always be checked against actual demand.
We now move to a sub-section: Process improvement frameworks.
Lean removes activities that do not create customer value.
The steps are: identify value, map the value stream, improve flow, use pull where appropriate, and continuously improve.
Waste includes waiting, unnecessary movement, excess inventory, defects and redundant processing.
Six Sigma reduces defects and process variation.
Its method is DMAIC, which means Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve and Control.
In practice, you define the problem, establish a baseline, identify root causes, implement improvements, and sustain the gains.
Lean Six Sigma combines waste reduction with variation reduction.
Business Process Reengineering, or BPR, radically redesigns workflows rather than making small improvements.
Total Quality Management, or TQM, builds organisation-wide commitment to continuous quality improvement and customer satisfaction.

For example, a claims department could use Lean to eliminate duplicate approvals, Six Sigma to reduce incorrect claims, BPR to replace a fragmented workflow with a unified digital process, and TQM to sustain quality across departments.
These approaches can complement one another.
The next sub-section is the Efficiency transformation roadmap.
First, map the existing workflow and establish baselines.
Then identify bottlenecks and root causes.
Prioritise improvements by value, feasibility and risk.
After that, redesign processes, select suitable tools, pilot with users, train staff, integrate systems, measure outcomes, and continuously improve.
Throughout, avoid automating broken processes unchanged.
Finally, a worked calculation.
Suppose processing time falls from 10 days to 2 days.
The reduction equals ten minus two, divided by ten, multiplied by one hundred percent.
That gives eighty percent.
Now suppose daily output rises from 100 to 150 claims with the same resources.
Throughput then increases by fifty percent.
But track quality as well: faster processing is not beneficial if rejection errors increase.
